The latest official SOFR print is 3.88 percent for Friday, October second, up one basis point from the prior day. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 begins around 6.88 percent before fees and hedging. At SOFR plus 350, it starts around 7.38 percent.

So the borrower sees two different pressures. Floating-rate carry is little changed. Fixed-rate proceeds are being tested by a long end that remains above five and a quarter percent. Unless net operating income rises or spreads compress, a higher 10-year yield means less debt for the same coverage requirement.

Monday's deal flow showed that capital is still getting out the door when the collateral and structure fit the lender.

The largest evidence came from Walker and Dunlop, which arranged roughly 631 million dollars of fixed-rate Fannie Mae loans for IMT Capital. The nine-property portfolio contains 3,528 apartments across Florida, Arizona, Texas, Colorado, California and Tennessee.

In a separate Florida transaction, April Housing completed a 366.1 million dollar Fannie Mae refinance across 13 apartment communities. April Housing is a Blackstone portfolio company focused on preserving affordable housing.

Together, those two announcements put nearly one billion dollars of fresh Fannie Mae multifamily financing into the Monday tape. That is meaningful proof of agency capacity, but the collateral also explains the execution. One portfolio offers geographic diversification and scale. The other combines affordable housing with a mission-driven borrower. Fannie and Freddie have room under their 2026 caps, yet they still reward clean operating history, defensible collections and transactions that fit housing goals.

Freddie Mac was active as well. Regions Bank arranged a 64 million dollar Freddie loan to refinance Elevate Rocky River, a stabilized 360-unit community near Charlotte. The permanent financing replaced construction debt after the property reached stabilization.

In Washington state, Northmarq arranged a 25.5 million dollar, seven-year fixed-rate Freddie Mac acquisition loan on Chambers Reserve, a 125-unit rental townhome community. Those deals show two familiar agency lanes: a construction takeout after lease-up and a permanent acquisition loan on a completed rental asset.

They also show why timing matters. A sponsor that reaches stabilization with clean trailing income can move from construction risk into long-term nonrecourse debt. A project that is still offering heavy concessions or carrying weak collections may not receive the same proceeds, even if physical occupancy looks strong.

Private credit covered a different part of the market. Madison Realty Capital provided a 127 million dollar construction takeout loan on The Arcadian, a newly delivered 502-unit apartment community in Fort Lauderdale. Berkadia arranged the financing.

That is a classic debt-fund use case: a large completed property needs time to season, but it is not yet ready for the permanent execution its sponsor ultimately wants. The lender can underwrite the lease-up and move quickly, while charging for that flexibility through spread, reserves and structure.

At a 3.88 percent SOFR base, a debt-fund quote at plus 350 starts near 7.38 percent, and plus 450 starts near 8.38 percent. The business plan has to create value faster than that coupon consumes the interest reserve. The exit cannot be a vague assumption that rates will fall. It needs a believable path to agency, life-company, bank or securitized debt based on stabilized income.

Banks remain active where relationships and property quality reduce uncertainty. Byline Bank closed a 20.25 million dollar term loan for Stockbridge Capital Group on a fully leased industrial outdoor-storage portfolio near the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Four Leaf Credit Union provided 15 million dollars on a 175-unit rent-stabilized apartment property in Brooklyn.

Those are smaller than the agency portfolios, but they are useful signals. Depository lenders are not absent. They are choosing transactions with identifiable cash flow, experienced sponsors and manageable hold exposure. Borrowers should expect more attention to deposits, guarantees, concentration and the lender's total relationship than they would receive from CMBS or an agency lender.

Life-company money remains available for stabilized assets at moderate leverage, but the benchmark math is demanding. The latest published Northmarq table showed 10-year life-company spreads around 140 to 190 basis points for lower-leverage commercial loans and 150 to 220 for higher leverage. Using Monday's 5.31 percent 10-year Treasury, that implies a rough coupon range beginning around the high sixes and extending into the mid sevens before deal-specific adjustments.

Life companies can still win on certainty, servicing and a clean fixed-rate structure. The constraint is proceeds. Their best quotes are likely to favor durable apartments, industrial, necessity retail and strong credit tenancy. Properties requiring operational improvement generally fit bank bridge or debt-fund capital better.

CMBS remains open, but the latest performance data give bond buyers reason to stay selective. Trepp reported that the overall CMBS delinquency rate rose 17 basis points in September to 8.02 percent, the highest since November 2020. Multifamily rose 35 basis points to 8.04 percent. Office climbed to 12.16 percent.

Five large newly delinquent loans drove much of the overall increase, including office, mixed-use and hotel collateral. That matters because it shows concentration can move the headline rate sharply. But the multifamily increase was broader, with loans in several states moving into 30-day delinquency.

For new borrowers, CMBS still offers nonrecourse proceeds and access for properties that do not fit agency or bank boxes. Indicative 10-year conduit spreads have recently been around 175 to 225 basis points, putting all-in rates roughly around seven to seven and a half percent against current benchmarks. The exact quote depends on leverage, property type, sponsorship and bond-market conditions.

The lesson is not that the securitization market is closed. It is that underwritten income, reserves and maturity protection receive more scrutiny when delinquencies rise. A transaction can clear while a weaker loan in the same property sector moves to special servicing.

HUD and FHA remain the slow but durable alternative for eligible multifamily. The 47 million dollar FHA 221(d)(4) financing for the planned 279-unit Vic at Sunterra in Katy remains the clearest current example. Its construction period rolls into a fully amortizing 40-year permanent term, removing the need for a separate takeout.

There was no equally large fresh HUD closing on Monday, so the meaningful update is competitive rather than transactional. With the 10-year Treasury at 5.31 and construction takeout risk expensive, long-duration federal execution becomes more valuable for sponsors who can absorb the documentation, mortgage insurance and processing time.

The lending mood is deteriorating even while large deals close. The CRE Finance Council's third-quarter sentiment index fell 17.5 percent to 83.3, its lowest level in three years. All nine core measures weakened, and 92 percent of surveyed finance executives said interest rates would weigh on the market.

That is the clearest summary of current execution. Liquidity exists, but confidence is lower. Banks want relationships and clean exposure. Life companies want stable cash flow and moderate leverage. Fannie and Freddie can execute at scale on qualifying multifamily. HUD offers duration. CMBS offers nonrecourse reach, and debt funds provide speed and transition capital at a premium.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The latest official 2-year Treasury is 4.84 percent, the 5-year is 5.06, the 10-year is 5.31 and the 30-year is 5.66. Latest official SOFR is 3.88 percent. The 2-to-30-year curve is 82 basis points, two basis points steeper than Friday.

One thing to watch is whether agency scale can keep overpowering the benchmark shock. Monday delivered nearly a billion dollars of announced Fannie Mae portfolio refinancings. If the 10-year Treasury keeps rising, ask whether Tuesday's lenders hold spreads, reduce proceeds or begin to retrade coupons. That answer will tell us more about real borrowing conditions than the headline availability of capital.

That is Debt Desk for Tuesday. We will be back tomorrow with the latest rates, structures and deals that make it across the finish line.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — October 5, 2026: A New Court Term and the Cost of Capital
item.description: The Coast Guard suspends its Nantucket search, a new Caribbean boat strike raises legal questions, Democrats stretch the House map and the Supreme Court opens a consequential term. Debt Desk covers the latest Treasury curve, SOFR and execution across banks, agencies, HUD, CMBS, life companies and debt funds.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Monday, October fifth.

The Coast Guard has suspended its search for the six people aboard an air ambulance that disappeared while flying from Bermuda to Boston, a grim new development in the story we followed through the weekend.

The Gulfstream G100 lost contact early Saturday after its pilot reported electrical trouble. Search crews later confirmed that debris found south of Nantucket came from the aircraft. On Sunday, officials said the active search was being suspended after crews covered more than 1,600 square miles by air and sea.

The plane carried four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals. They included the patient, a relative, two medical personnel and two pilots. Authorities had not announced finding any survivors when the suspension was reported.

The investigation now moves from an urgent rescue effort toward determining what happened. The National Transportation Safety Board has been gathering information, and investigators will be looking at the reported electrical problems, the weather, flight data and any wreckage that can be recovered. For the families, the end of the active search is not the end of the questions.

The United States military says it struck another suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean on Sunday, killing four people. Southern Command said the vessel was traveling along a known trafficking route, and the military released video showing an explosion destroying what it described as a go-fast boat.

The government did not publicly provide evidence that the boat was carrying drugs or identify the people who were killed. The latest strike brings the reported death toll from this campaign to at least 235 people across 70 attacks since September of last year.

The operation has grown well beyond an occasional interdiction. The administration says the United States is in an armed conflict with cartels and argues that military force is necessary to disrupt trafficking and reduce overdose deaths. Critics in Congress and the legal community question the evidence, the lack of judicial process and the legal basis for treating people suspected of smuggling as wartime targets.

The administration is also pursuing agreements that would allow joint operations on land in parts of Latin America. That makes the immediate question larger than one boat. Watch for demands that the White House disclose its intelligence and legal rationale, and for any response from governments in the region.

With Election Day four weeks away, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Sunday that his party is reaching into districts President Trump carried in 2024 as it tries to win control of the chamber.

Jeffries compared the strategy with the Democratic wave of 2018, when the party flipped dozens of Republican seats during Trump's first term. The current map is harder in important ways. Republicans have a fundraising advantage, and redistricting has reduced the number of obvious swing districts. Still, Democrats believe voter frustration over prices and the economy gives them a chance in places that would normally be considered safely Republican.

That claim will be tested against the president's near-daily campaign schedule. Trump heads to Nebraska today, following stops in Alabama and Ohio that we covered over the weekend. The Nebraska visit comes with a local complication: ranchers are unhappy with his proposal to import more beef as part of an effort to lower grocery prices.

The national political argument is becoming clearer. Republicans are asking their base to protect the administration's agenda. Democrats are trying to make the election a referendum on affordability and executive power. Candidate travel, outside spending and early-vote patterns will show whether either side is expanding the map or simply projecting confidence.

The Supreme Court begins its new term today, and the first argument is the Boulder climate case we previewed Sunday. The city and county of Boulder want ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to help pay costs associated with climate-related disasters. The companies say state lawsuits cannot be used to regulate emissions produced around the world and argue that the issue belongs under federal law.

The court's handling of jurisdiction could decide whether similar state-law cases around the country move forward. Justice Samuel Alito is recused, leaving eight justices and the possibility of an evenly divided court.

The broader term also includes major disputes over immigration, voting, religious rights and firearms. The justices are expected to consider whether migrants sent to countries where they have no ties must receive a chance to object, and whether immigrants who have lived in the United States for years can be detained without a bond hearing.

Later in the term, the court will hear challenges to Arizona voting rules and state bans on semiautomatic rifles. The first day therefore opens with one climate case, but the docket as a whole could reshape federal power and individual rights well beyond this election.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk.

Markets reopen this morning with the commercial real estate industry still digesting an unusually steep and expensive Treasury curve. The latest official close is Friday, October second: 4.83 percent on the 2-year, 5.06 percent on the 5-year, 5.28 percent on the 10-year and 5.63 percent on the 30-year.

Nothing newer printed over the weekend. That is important because Monday borrowers should compare live lender quotes with Friday's verified close, not with an indicative screen that moved in thin overnight trading.

The shape of the curve tells the real story. The 5-year sits 23 basis points above the 2-year. The 10-year is 22 basis points above the 5-year, and the 30-year is another 35 basis points above the 10-year. The gap from 2 years to 30 years is 80 basis points.

A softer employment report would normally encourage borrowers to expect rate relief. Friday showed why that assumption can fail. The front end reflects expectations for Federal Reserve policy, while the 10- and 30-year points also carry inflation risk, Treasury supply and term premium. If investors demand more compensation to hold long bonds, permanent commercial mortgage rates can remain high even when the market expects easier short-term policy later.

The latest official SOFR print is 3.87 percent for October 1, three basis points below the previous day. That is modest help for floating-rate borrowers, not a reset of the economics. A loan priced at SOFR plus 300 basis points begins around 6.87 percent before fees and hedging. At a 350-basis-point spread, the starting coupon is about 7.37 percent.

For a transitional apartment project, those numbers still put pressure on debt-service coverage and interest reserves. They also make the extension decision more consequential. Paying another extension fee and buying a new cap may preserve the business plan, but only if lease-up or net operating income can close the gap before the next maturity.

The weekend did not produce a new large closing that displaced the transactions reported Friday. The most useful deals therefore remain evidence of where capital is actually clearing, not fresh Monday headlines.

In Nashville, Helaba provided a 105 million dollar bridge loan on Modera Riverview, a completed 400-unit apartment property. The financing replaced a 103 million dollar PNC construction loan. That is an instructive bank execution: a completed asset, experienced sponsorship, leased retail and a defined path through stabilization.

Banks are lending, but the lane is narrow. Relationship deposits, recourse and clean construction exposure can improve a quote. They do not substitute for coverage, equity or a credible exit. Regional and money-center banks are most competitive when the borrower can show durable cash flow or a short list of specific milestones rather than a general hope that rents rise and rates fall.

Life companies are operating with similar selectivity at lower leverage. Stabilized apartments, industrial assets and grocery-anchored retail can attract long-duration, fixed-rate money. The advantage is certainty and often cleaner servicing. The constraint is proceeds. With the 5-year Treasury above five percent and the 10-year above five and a quarter, even a disciplined spread produces a coupon that limits leverage.

Indicative lender tables over the weekend put that pressure into practical terms. Bank and life-company quotes may carry relatively tight spreads for the strongest assets, yet the elevated benchmark still pushes all-in fixed coupons into a range that can reduce acquisition proceeds. CMBS and private-credit quotes can preserve leverage, but they charge for that flexibility through wider spreads, reserves or structure. Sponsors are increasingly solving the difference with more equity, seller financing or preferred capital. Each choice protects senior debt coverage, but each also changes the return profile and the control rights around the property.

That is why quote comparison needs to go beyond rate. A borrower should examine amortization, interest-only periods, cash management, reserves, prepayment and the lender's ability to hold terms through closing. A tighter spread does not automatically produce a better execution if proceeds are lower or the prepayment structure conflicts with the business plan.

In multifamily, Freddie Mac provided a strong permanent-debt comparison with a 75 million dollar fixed-rate refinance on EVO St. Petersburg, a 334-unit apartment tower completed in 2023. Walker and Dunlop arranged the loan.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain reliable sources of nonrecourse liquidity, especially for stabilized properties with clean operating histories. But agency does not mean automatic maximum leverage. Loans are being sized to in-place income, current coupons and required coverage. Affordability features may improve pricing or mission treatment, while weak collections, elevated concessions or rising insurance costs can reduce proceeds.

The annual multifamily purchase caps are 88 billion dollars for each enterprise in 2026, with workforce-housing loans excluded from the limits and at least half of capped business required to be mission-driven. The caps create room to lend. They do not require Fannie or Freddie to overlook property-level risk.

Borrowers should compare agency quotes on total economics. Yield maintenance, defeasance, supplemental-loan options, replacement reserves and the ability to transfer the debt can matter as much as a few basis points in coupon. That is especially true for owners who may sell before maturity.

HUD also remains relevant where certainty matters more than speed. Dwight Capital's 47 million dollar FHA 221(d)(4) loan for The Vic at Sunterra in Katy, Texas, finances a planned 279-unit development. The structure includes a 24-month interest-only construction period followed by a fully amortizing 40-year term.

That combination removes the need to secure a separate permanent takeout after lease-up. The tradeoff is the longer federal process, mortgage insurance and detailed program requirements. For an eligible development, however, eliminating future refinance risk can be more valuable than closing quickly with floating-rate bridge debt.

Debt funds continue to own the faster, more flexible end of construction and transition. Apollo's 130.5 million dollar loan for a logistics project in Rialto, California, and SCALE Lending's 67.5 million dollar apartment construction loan in Rahway, New Jersey, show private credit funding business plans that banks may find too concentrated or operationally complex.

The trade is cost. A debt-fund loan quoted over SOFR can land in the high sevens, eights or higher before exit fees and extensions. The right question is not simply whether the lender will close. It is whether the project has enough interest reserve, enough equity and a realistic takeout once it reaches its next milestone.

CMBS is open, but bond buyers are making sharper distinctions. A JPMorgan-led group is preparing a roughly 1.77 billion dollar refinancing on a large Midtown Manhattan office property. The transaction will test investor appetite for scale and office exposure. Tenant rollover, appraisal assumptions, reserves and extension protections will matter as much as the headline coupon.

For multifamily borrowers, conduit execution remains useful when an asset falls outside agency rules or when nonrecourse proceeds are the priority. The cost is securitization-market volatility, reserve requirements and restrictive prepayment. Reported September CMBS delinquency above eight percent is also keeping investors focused on maturity risk and the credibility of underwritten income.

The practical Monday tone is available but disciplined. Banks favor relationships and lower-risk transitions. Life companies favor stabilized cash flow and moderate leverage. Agencies offer dependable apartment liquidity but size to reality. HUD offers duration and construction-to-permanent certainty for borrowers able to navigate the process. CMBS provides scale and nonrecourse proceeds, while debt funds sell speed and flexibility at a premium.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The latest official 2-year Treasury is 4.83 percent, the 5-year is 5.06, the 10-year is 5.28 and the 30-year is 5.63. Latest official SOFR is 3.87 percent. At Friday's close, the S and P 500 gained seven tenths of a percent, the Dow added one half percent and the Nasdaq rose 1.2 percent.

One thing to watch is whether today's Treasury move reaches the middle and long end of the curve. If the 2-year falls while the 5-, 10- and 30-year yields stay elevated, floating-rate borrowers may see incremental relief while permanent-loan coupons remain stubborn. If the rally broadens, borrowers with active quotes should ask immediately whether the lower benchmark changes the coupon, proceeds or both, and whether the lender's spread is moving in the opposite direction.

That is Debt Desk for Monday. We will be back tomorrow with the latest rates, structures and deals that make it across the finish line.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — October 4, 2026: Medicare Checks, Campaign Pressure and a Steep CRE Curve
item.description: New Medicare payments, an Ohio campaign stop, an Atlantic air-ambulance search and a major Supreme Court climate case lead the national brief. Debt Desk examines the latest Treasury curve, SOFR, multifamily financing and execution across banks, life companies, CMBS, agencies, HUD and debt funds.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Sunday, October fourth.

The White House is promising a one-time 90-dollar payment to more than 20 million Medicare beneficiaries, putting affordability and direct payments back at the center of the midterm campaign.

President Trump announced the plan late Friday. The administration says eligible Medicare Part B enrollees will receive the money in October by direct deposit or check, with funding coming from the Medicare Improvement Fund. That fund was created by Congress in 2008 to support program operations and payments to healthcare providers.

There are important limits. The payment is for beneficiaries living in the United States who are not already receiving premium assistance through Medicaid and are not paying income-adjusted premiums. Medicare Advantage members are also excluded. Because more than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Advantage, the reach is substantial but far from universal.

The announcement follows separate promises of 500-dollar Affordable Care Act rebates for about one million people and 5,000-dollar payments to every American adult if Republicans keep control of Congress. That larger pledge would require congressional approval and could cost more than one trillion dollars. The 90-dollar Medicare payment is smaller and the administration says it can act under existing authority.

The political point is unmistakable. Polling has shown broad frustration with gasoline, grocery and healthcare costs. The White House is trying to turn that frustration into visible relief before the November third election. The policy question is whether using a flexible Medicare fund for direct premium help withstands scrutiny and whether voters see a one-time payment as meaningful against recurring household expenses.

Trump carried the affordability message to Vandalia, Ohio, Saturday night, but his rally also exposed the tension around artificial intelligence and power demand. He defended the rapid buildout of data centers, arguing that Ohio should capture the investment and jobs rather than lose projects to China.

The response in the room was notably quieter than it was for the president's other themes. Data centers have become a difficult local issue because they promise construction, tax revenue and technology investment while also consuming enormous amounts of electricity and water. Communities worry that new generation and grid upgrades will show up in household utility bills.

Trump was campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted in a close race. He praised Husted for trying to advance legislation on data-center costs, even though that effort did not move forward. The stop continues the campaign push we followed Friday in Alabama, but with a sharper economic contrast. Ohio is a state the president has carried comfortably, yet the party is defending a competitive Senate seat amid weak national approval on the cost of living.

The immediate watch is whether Republicans can separate support for artificial-intelligence investment from voter anger about electricity bills. That argument will matter beyond Ohio because data-center construction is reshaping power planning, land use and capital spending across the country.

Off the Massachusetts coast, the Coast Guard found a debris field while searching for an air ambulance that disappeared early Saturday on a flight from Bermuda to Boston. Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard the Gulfstream G100, including four crew members and two passengers.

The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the aircraft approached the coast. Air-traffic audio suggested the crew may have lost navigational instruments as a storm stood in its path. Preliminary tracking data showed the jet descending sharply from about 24,000 feet to roughly 10,000 feet.

A Coast Guard cutter continued searching through the night and into Sunday. The National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information, while Canadian and Bermudian authorities were coordinating with the United States. The discovery of debris changes the character of the operation, but officials had not announced the recovery of anyone aboard as of early Sunday.

The final national story looks ahead to the Supreme Court's new term. On Monday, the justices are scheduled to hear a case brought by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, against ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy. Boulder says the companies misled the public about their contribution to climate change and should help pay local costs associated with worsening disasters.

The dispute grew more consequential after the 2021 Marshall Fire, which caused an estimated two billion dollars in damage and became the costliest wildfire in Colorado history. Similar lawsuits are pending around the country, so the court's decision could determine whether state-law claims of this kind proceed or are displaced by federal authority.

The companies, backed by the Trump administration, argue that a patchwork of state suits would effectively regulate global emissions and intrude on the federal government's role under the Clean Air Act. Boulder says it is seeking compensation for local harm, not setting national emissions policy.

Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself because he owns stock in oil companies, leaving eight justices and the possibility of a tie. The court could also avoid the broad climate question by deciding that it lacks jurisdiction at this stage. Either way, the argument will be one of the first major signals from the court's new term.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk, where the latest available market close still shows a steep and expensive curve.

The official Treasury close for Friday, October second, was 4.83 percent on the 2-year, 5.06 percent on the 5-year, 5.28 percent on the 10-year and 5.63 percent on the 30-year. Those are the latest official prints available over the weekend.

The term structure matters. The 5-year is 23 basis points above the 2-year. The 10-year is another 22 basis points above the 5-year, and the 30-year sits 35 basis points above the 10-year. From 2 years to 30 years, the curve rises 80 basis points.

Friday's weak employment report did not deliver the fixed-rate relief borrowers might have expected. The front end can respond to a softer labor market and a more patient Federal Reserve, while the long end continues to absorb inflation risk, heavy government borrowing and term premium. That split is why a borrower cannot translate a weaker jobs number directly into a cheaper five-, seven- or ten-year commercial mortgage.

The latest official SOFR print is 3.87 percent for October first, down three basis points from the prior day. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 300 basis points starts near 6.87 percent before fees and hedging. At a 350-basis-point spread, it begins near 7.37 percent. The daily improvement is welcome, but it is not large enough to fix a coverage shortfall or eliminate the cost of a rate cap.

The most useful fresh evidence comes from multifamily loans that crossed the finish line late in the week. In Nashville, Helaba provided a 105 million dollar bridge loan on Modera Riverview, a completed 400-unit apartment property with ground-floor retail. The new financing replaced a 103 million dollar PNC construction loan.

This is a bank execution, but not a return to loose bank lending. The asset is complete, the sponsor group is experienced and the retail space is leased. Helaba is taking measured stabilization risk after construction, with a defined path toward permanent financing. That is where banks remain competitive: strong sponsorship, visible collateral and a believable exit.

For other borrowers, banks are still sensitive to construction concentrations, office exposure, deposits and recourse. Relationship value can improve a quote, but it does not erase debt-service coverage or loan-to-cost discipline. Banks will stretch selectively for the clients and assets they want, not for a business plan that depends on immediate rent growth.

Freddie Mac supplied the clearest permanent-debt comparison. Front Range Capital Partners secured a 75 million dollar fixed-rate refinance on EVO St. Petersburg, a 334-unit apartment tower completed in 2023. Walker and Dunlop arranged the financing.

The transaction shows the agency market doing what it does best: placing long-duration, nonrecourse capital on newer multifamily with sufficient operating history. Freddie and Fannie remain active, but proceeds are being sized to actual net operating income and current coupons. Strong, lower-leverage properties can still reach the six-percent range. Higher leverage, weaker coverage or operational complexity can push the all-in rate toward seven percent and reduce proceeds.

Borrowers comparing Fannie and Freddie executions should look beyond the headline spread. The real comparison includes proceeds, amortization, interest-only periods, replacement reserves, affordability incentives and prepayment structure. A lower coupon with restrictive defeasance or yield maintenance may not be the best fit for a sponsor that expects to sell or refinance early.

HUD also produced a meaningful multifamily closing. Dwight Capital completed a 47 million dollar FHA 221(d)(4) loan for The Vic at Sunterra, a planned 279-unit community in Katy, Texas. The nonrecourse financing includes a 24-month interest-only construction period followed by a fully amortizing 40-year term.

That structure removes the need for a separate permanent takeout after construction. In a market where a two-year business plan can meet a completely different yield curve at stabilization, that certainty has real value. The cost is a slower, more documentation-heavy process with mortgage insurance and federal requirements. HUD is not the fastest lane, but for eligible projects it can solve both construction and refinance risk in one closing.

Debt funds continue to dominate the faster and more transitional end of the market. Apollo's 130.5 million dollar construction loan for a Rialto, California, logistics project and SCALE Lending's 67.5 million dollar apartment construction loan in Rahway, New Jersey, were the latest large examples. There was no material weekend update to either transaction, so the continuing signal matters more than the individual deal details.

Private credit is available when a sponsor needs speed, leverage or flexibility that a regulated bank may not provide. The trade is price. A debt fund spread over SOFR can quickly create an all-in coupon in the high sevens, eights or above, and extensions, exit fees and interest reserves affect the true cost. The best executions have a specific milestone and a credible takeout, not simply a hope that rates fall.

Life companies occupy the opposite end of the risk spectrum. They remain competitive on stabilized apartments, industrial, grocery-anchored retail and other durable cash flow at moderate leverage. With the 5-year Treasury at 5.06 percent and the 10-year at 5.28, even an attractive spread produces a coupon that challenges acquisition leverage. Life companies offer duration and rate certainty, but they will generally stop proceeds before coverage becomes thin.

CMBS remains open for borrowers seeking nonrecourse capital, scale or flexibility outside the agency and life-company boxes. The developing 1.77 billion dollar Midtown Manhattan office refinance remains an important test of large-loan demand, though final pricing was not reported over the weekend. Bond buyers will focus on tenant rollover, reserves, valuation and extension protections.

In multifamily CMBS, the market is useful when an asset does not fit agency eligibility or a borrower prioritizes proceeds. The tradeoffs include securitization volatility, reserve requirements and often restrictive prepayment. September's reported CMBS delinquency rate moving above eight percent adds to investor caution, especially for office and maturity-sensitive collateral. That does not close the market, but it raises the premium for stories that require optimistic assumptions.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The latest official 2-year Treasury is 4.83 percent, the 5-year is 5.06, the 10-year is 5.28 and the 30-year is 5.63. Latest official SOFR is 3.87 percent. Friday's stock session was positive, with the S and P 500 up seven tenths of a percent, the Dow up one half percent and the Nasdaq up 1.2 percent. Risk assets welcomed the softer jobs report, while the Treasury close reminded borrowers that long-term financing costs have their own drivers.

One thing to watch is Monday's reaction across the full curve. If the weak payroll report pulls the 2-year lower but leaves the 10- and 30-year yields elevated, floating-rate borrowers may get incremental relief while permanent-loan coupons remain stubborn. If the rally reaches the 5- and 10-year points, borrowers with live quotes should ask lenders how quickly the benchmark improvement flows through and whether spreads or proceeds change at the same time.

That is Debt Desk for Sunday. We will be back tomorrow with the latest rates, structures and deals that make it across the finish line.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — October 3, 2026: Jobs Slow, Fuel Reserves Open and Rates Stay High
item.description: A weak September jobs report, a coordinated G7 fuel release and a border-wall injunction lead the national brief. Debt Desk examines Friday’s higher Treasury close, lower SOFR, fresh multifamily financing and execution across banks, life companies, CMBS, agencies, HUD and debt funds.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Saturday, October third.

The American job market lost more momentum than expected in September, giving the Federal Reserve a little more room to wait before raising rates again and giving voters another reason to question the strength of the economy.

Employers added 29,000 jobs last month. That was far below the roughly 90,000 economists expected and down sharply from a revised 133,000 in August. The unemployment rate moved up one tenth of a percentage point to 4.2 percent. Revisions also removed 60,000 jobs from the combined July and August totals.

The details describe a labor market that is not collapsing, but is becoming harder to enter. Nearly half a million people joined the labor force, which helped push unemployment higher. Healthcare added 17,000 jobs, construction added 11,000 and manufacturing added 9,000. Government employment fell by 17,000, while professional and business services lost 9,000.

Wage growth cooled as well. Average hourly earnings were up 3 percent from a year ago, the smallest annual increase since May 2021. That reduces one source of inflation pressure, although it does not erase the burden of high prices already facing households.

This is the last monthly employment report before the November third midterm election. It lands against consumer confidence at a decade low and polling that shows deep dissatisfaction with the cost of living. President Trump can point to continued job creation and historically low layoffs. His opponents can point to weak hiring, downward revisions and the difficulty unemployed workers face finding a new position. For the Federal Reserve, the report supports patience. For households, it confirms that the economy feels less secure than the unemployment rate alone suggests.

The second major development is an international attempt to bring down fuel prices. The Group of Seven nations says it will release 100 million barrels of oil and refined products in the coming weeks, beginning with a substantial amount of diesel within 20 days and completing the broader release over four months.

The move follows record diesel prices in the United States and Europe. The national U.S. average was 6 dollars and 37 cents a gallon Friday after reaching 6 dollars and 52 cents in late September. The Iran war has disrupted Persian Gulf shipments, while Russia’s export restrictions have tightened an already stressed global market.

President Trump said the release would begin immediately and ruled out a ban on U.S. diesel exports, an idea some Republicans had promoted. The announcement pushed oil lower early Friday, though prices recovered much of that decline as traders questioned whether the 100 million barrels are additional supply or part of a reserve release already announced in March.

This is a meaningful new chapter in the energy story we have been following. The administration is trying to create visible relief before the election without restricting trade. The practical test is whether diesel inventories arrive quickly enough to lower trucking, farming and distribution costs. Even a modest decline would matter because diesel prices work their way through almost every physical supply chain.

The campaign itself is entering a more urgent phase. Trump rallied in Mobile, Alabama, Friday and travels to Ohio today as Republicans confront weak economic approval and a difficult congressional map. The president urged support for Republican candidates in Alabama, but his choice to spend time in a deeply Republican state highlights concern about turnout among his own voters.

The money is moving with the map. The Senate Leadership Fund plans to spend more than 8 million dollars in Kansas while pulling back from North Carolina, where Trump acknowledged concern about Republican candidate Michael Whatley. A month before Election Day, those shifts suggest Republican strategists are spending to protect territory that once looked safer.

And a federal judge has temporarily blocked the administration from building a border wall and related infrastructure through the Big Bend region of Texas. Landowners, businesses and environmental groups challenged the project, which is part of a broader 46 billion dollar border infrastructure program.

Judge Kathleen Cardone found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on at least one claim and faced irreparable harm without an injunction. The ruling includes Big Bend National Park. Customs and Border Protection says it remains confident in its legal authority and is considering next steps with the Justice Department.

The order does not settle the larger case, and it does not stop the administration’s border program nationwide. It does create a fresh legal barrier in one of the most environmentally sensitive and geographically remote parts of the border. Watch whether the government appeals and whether the court narrows or extends the injunction.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk, where the jobs report produced a brief rally, but official closing yields still finished higher across the curve.

The official Treasury close for October second was 4.83 percent on the 2-year, 5.06 percent on the 5-year, 5.28 percent on the 10-year and 5.63 percent on the 30-year. Compared with Thursday, the 2-year and 5-year each rose five basis points, the 10-year rose four and the 30-year rose two.

The curve remains upward sloping. The 10-year is 45 basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year is 80 basis points above it. That shape matters as much as the daily move. The weak jobs report softened expectations for another near-term Fed increase, but inflation, energy prices, federal borrowing and term premium are keeping longer yields elevated.

For commercial real estate borrowers, the takeaway is uncomfortable but clear. Softer hiring may restrain the policy rate, yet it has not produced durable relief in the fixed-rate benchmarks used to price permanent debt. A quote tied to the 5-year or 10-year Treasury is still sitting near the highest levels of this cycle. A borrower waiting only for the Fed may miss the separate risk embedded in the long end.

The latest official SOFR print is 3.87 percent for October 1, down three basis points from the prior day. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 350 basis points therefore begins around 7.37 percent before fees, reserves and the cost of a rate cap. The change is welcome, but three basis points will not rescue a thin debt-service coverage ratio. Structure, proceeds and hedging cost remain decisive.

Fresh deal activity shows lenders are still distinguishing sharply between stabilized cash flow and transitional risk. In Nashville, German commercial bank Helaba provided a 105 million dollar bridge loan to CrossHarbor Capital Partners and Mill Creek Residential for Modera Riverview, a 400-unit apartment property with nearly 14,000 square feet of retail.

The financing takes out a 103 million dollar PNC construction loan after the property opened in 2024. That is exactly the kind of transition the market needs to see: construction debt moving into a bridge facility as a new asset seasons, with a well-capitalized sponsor and fully leased ground-floor retail strengthening the story. It is also a reminder that banks are lending when the property, sponsorship and exit path line up.

The rate environment still makes that exit path demanding. Helaba is accepting lease-up and stabilization risk, but the building is complete. The next refinancing will depend on occupancy, rent growth and a permanent lender’s underwritten net operating income. Bridge capital can buy time; it cannot manufacture coverage.

Freddie Mac supplied another clear permanent-debt execution. Front Range Capital Partners obtained 75 million dollars of fixed-rate financing on EVO St. Petersburg, a 23-story, 334-unit apartment tower delivered in 2023. Walker and Dunlop arranged the loan.

This deal shows the agency lane functioning as intended for newer stabilized multifamily. Freddie can offer fixed-rate, nonrecourse capital when operations support the requested proceeds. That can be a cleaner fit than bank debt for a sponsor seeking duration, and usually a lower-cost fit than a debt fund once the business plan has moved beyond construction and lease-up.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain active, but they are not ignoring the Treasury move. Broad agency coupons are generally landing in the sixes for strong, lower-leverage properties, with higher leverage, weaker coverage or more complicated assets pushing execution toward seven percent. Borrowers comparing agency quotes should focus on actual proceeds, prepayment flexibility and required reserves, not merely the headline spread.

HUD produced a new construction execution as well. Dwight Capital closed a 47 million dollar FHA 221(d)(4) loan for The Vic at Sunterra, a planned 279-unit apartment community in Katy, Texas. The nonrecourse financing includes a 24-month interest-only period followed by a fully amortizing 40-year term.

That long amortization is the central advantage. A conventional construction loan usually leaves a borrower exposed to a new credit decision and a new rate environment at stabilization. The HUD structure carries through construction into permanent debt. The tradeoff is a slower, documentation-heavy process, along with mortgage insurance and federal requirements. For sponsors that can meet those requirements, removing refinance risk for four decades is unusually valuable in this market.

Debt funds remain the most visible providers of construction and transition capital where speed and leverage matter. Apollo’s 130.5 million dollar industrial construction loan in Rialto and SCALE Lending’s 67.5 million dollar second-phase apartment loan in Rahway remain the clearest recent examples. Neither received a material update Friday, so there is no reason to replay the deal details. The continuing signal is that private credit will fund a defined business plan when a bank is constrained, but borrowers pay for certainty and flexibility.

Life companies are on the other side of that spectrum. They are most competitive on stabilized apartments, industrial, grocery-anchored retail and other durable cash flows at moderate leverage. With the 5-year at 5.06 percent and the 10-year at 5.28, even a disciplined spread produces a coupon that can challenge acquisition math. Life-company execution still offers rate certainty and long duration, but proceeds often stop where coverage becomes thin.

Banks are more varied. Relationship banks continue to compete for experienced sponsors, deposits and lower-leverage properties. Larger institutions can make construction-to-bridge transitions like the Nashville loan, while regional and community banks remain selective about office, construction concentrations and loans that require optimistic rent growth. The market is open, but the credit box is narrow.

CMBS remains available for scale and nonrecourse execution, though the recent Treasury volatility raises the cost of waiting through a securitization process. The developing 1.77 billion dollar Midtown Manhattan office refinancing still has not reported final pricing. Better Manhattan leasing helps the collateral narrative, but bond buyers will concentrate on tenant rollover, valuation, reserves and extension protections.

For multifamily, CMBS is most relevant when an asset does not fit agency rules or a borrower needs proceeds and flexibility that a life company will not offer. Coupons around seven percent or higher can still clear for the right transaction, but securitization volatility, defeasance and reserve requirements belong in the comparison. No major new multifamily CMBS issue displaced the fresh agency and HUD closings in Friday’s news cycle.

Here is the markets snapshot. The 2-year Treasury is 4.83 percent, the 5-year is 5.06, the 10-year is 5.28 and the 30-year is 5.63. Latest official SOFR is 3.87 percent. Stocks rose Friday, with the S and P 500 up seven tenths of a percent, the Dow up half a percent and the Nasdaq up 1.2 percent. The weak jobs report reduced immediate rate-hike pressure, but Treasuries finished with higher yields and the long end remains expensive.

One thing to watch is whether Friday’s employment data changes lender behavior before it changes benchmark rates. If debt providers see slower hiring as a reason to protect proceeds and underwrite softer rent growth, a future rate rally may not translate dollar for dollar into better leverage. If competition stays strong while SOFR drifts lower, floating-rate and bridge borrowers could gain a little negotiating room even with the 10-year above 5 percent.

That is Debt Desk for Saturday. We will be back tomorrow with the rates, the structures and the deals that make it across the finish line.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — October 2, 2026: Iran Deployment, Energy Costs and a Bond-Market Rally
item.description: A major U.S. naval buildup raises the stakes with Iran as new analysis sharpens the energy-cost debate. Debt Desk examines lower Treasury yields, a higher SOFR print, fresh private-credit construction loans, and current execution across banks, life companies, CMBS, agencies and HUD.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Friday, October second.

The United States is sending a third aircraft carrier and roughly 9,000 additional sailors and Marines toward the Middle East as President Trump weighs whether to resume a broader bombing campaign against Iran.

The Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the Makin Island amphibious group are now heading to the region. Together, the ships carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines. If the deployment proceeds as expected, the United States could have three carriers in the region by the end of October, with more than 20,000 sailors and Marines at sea nearby.

This is a meaningful new development in the Iran story. Trump said Thursday that he rejected Tehran’s latest ceasefire proposal and that an escalation after the November third midterm election remains possible. The force movement gives the president more options, but it also raises the risk that a miscalculation, an attack on shipping or an incident involving American personnel widens the conflict before diplomacy produces a durable result.

The economic consequences are already reaching beyond the region. Higher gasoline prices are squeezing household budgets, complicating the inflation outlook and feeding public frustration at home. The immediate question is whether the deployment is leverage for negotiations or preparation for a longer military campaign.

Energy affordability is also back in focus this morning. A new analysis from the nonpartisan group Energy Innovation estimates that federal policy changes since Trump returned to office will add an average of about 6,500 dollars to household energy costs through 2040 in the contiguous United States.

The study points to reduced clean-energy incentives, looser fuel-economy requirements and federal action against some wind, solar and hydrogen projects. It argues that those moves increase demand for natural gas and gasoline and eventually raise prices. The White House disputes that conclusion and says greater reliance on coal and natural gas will make the grid more reliable and reverse the effects of prior policy.

The argument lands at a sensitive moment. Residential electricity prices have continued to rise, data centers are increasing power demand, and the Iran conflict has pushed fuel costs higher. The estimate is a model, not a household bill that has already arrived. But it turns yesterday’s Washington debate over grid costs and permitting into a direct pocketbook issue.

Trade ministers from the Group of 20 also left Milwaukee without an agreement on how to address excess industrial capacity. The Trump administration says heavily subsidized overproduction, especially from China, depresses prices and hurts American manufacturers in steel, autos, batteries, paper and semiconductors.

Most governments at the meeting agreed the issue deserves action, but they did not agree on a common response. They also failed to bridge the worsening dispute between the United States and Canada. The administration imposed 50 percent tariffs on about 20 billion dollars of Canadian imports this summer and this week banned nearly another billion dollars of goods. Canada has retaliated.

That lack of progress matters because businesses do not need another declaration that trade is uncertain. They need rules that help them price inventory, plan investment and decide where to build. With no consensus, tariffs and national responses remain the operating framework.

And the political pressure behind those policies is becoming clearer. New polling from the Associated Press and the NORC Center finds that only 26 percent of adults approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, while just 17 percent approve of his handling of the cost of living.

The labor market looks better on paper than that mood suggests. Economists expect today’s September jobs report to show about 90,000 jobs added and unemployment holding near 4.1 percent. Layoffs remain relatively rare. But hiring is slow, the average unemployed worker is spending longer out of work, and consumer confidence has fallen to its lowest level in more than a decade.

Trump opened his final-month campaign push Thursday by promising that every adult citizen could receive a 5,000-dollar dividend if Republicans retain Congress. Such a program would require legislation and could cost roughly 1.2 trillion dollars. For voters, the contrast is now sharp: solid headline employment, weak confidence, expensive energy and a campaign promise whose financing has not been explained.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk, where Treasury yields finally moved lower across the curve, but floating-rate borrowers received a small move in the other direction.

The official Treasury close for October first was 4.78 percent on the 2-year, 5.01 percent on the 5-year, 5.24 percent on the 10-year and 5.61 percent on the 30-year. Compared with Wednesday, the 2-year fell 10 basis points, the 5-year fell eight, the 10-year fell five and the 30-year fell three.

That is a rally, but it is also another steepening move. The 10-year finished 46 basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year finished 83 basis points above it. Short maturities rallied the most as investors moved toward today’s jobs report. The long end offered less relief, preserving the market’s concern about inflation, federal borrowing and duration risk.

For commercial real estate, five basis points off the 10-year helps a fixed-rate quote. It does not reverse the rise of the past week. The 10-year is still seven basis points above last Friday’s close, while the 30-year is 12 basis points higher. Borrowers should read Thursday as a better day for execution, not as confirmation that long-term financing costs have broken lower.

The latest official SOFR print is 3.90 percent for September thirtieth, up two basis points. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 350 basis points now starts around 7.40 percent before fees, reserves and the cost of a cap. The overnight benchmark remains below longer Treasuries, but that does not automatically make floating debt cheaper after the lender spread and hedging expense are added.

Two fresh construction loans show where private credit is willing to take risk. Apollo provided 130.5 million dollars for Brookfield to build the Locust Gateway Logistics Center in Rialto, California. The five-year package finances a planned 664,859-square-foot industrial property on part of the former Rialto Airport.

The Inland Empire has had to work through heavy new supply and softer fundamentals, so the loan is not a generic vote on every warehouse development. It is a sponsor-specific, site-specific execution. Brookfield brings scale, Apollo can structure around construction and lease-up risk, and a five-year term gives the property time to deliver and season before a permanent exit.

The deal also shows the debt-fund advantage in today’s market. Private lenders can provide larger proceeds, flexible draws and certainty when a bank is constrained by construction exposure or when a life company wants stabilized income. The price is generally higher, but certainty can be more valuable than the lowest theoretical coupon.

Slate Property Group’s SCALE Lending made the second fresh loan, providing 67.5 million dollars for the 200-unit second phase of Meridia Rahway Brownstones in New Jersey. The 30-month financing includes two six-month extension options. It will retire existing senior debt and fund the rest of construction.

This is a more seasoned development story than a project starting from zero. The sponsor delivered the 298-unit first phase in 2022, giving the lender operating evidence at the location. The second phase adds apartments, a small retail component and substantial parking. That history can support a private-credit execution even while the new phase still carries completion and lease-up risk.

For banks, the tone remains selective rather than closed. Relationship lenders are most competitive when they receive deposits, guarantees, tax-credit economics or a path to permanent takeout. Yesterday’s affordable-housing stack in Paulsboro, New Jersey, remains a useful example: Citizens funded construction, Freddie Mac supplied long-term tax-exempt debt and low-income housing tax-credit equity filled the capital stack.

There was no comparably large new bank balance-sheet closing in the fresh cycle. That absence is informative. Banks can still win lower-leverage acquisitions, owner-user properties and relationship business, but private lenders are taking much of the visible construction and transitional volume.

Life companies remain strongest on stabilized assets, conservative leverage and borrowers who value rate certainty. Current market indications place many five- and ten-year life-company multifamily coupons in the mid-sixes, with spreads varying meaningfully by leverage and asset quality. The small Treasury rally improves those quotes at the margin.

The recent MetLife construction loan in suburban Boston also shows that life companies will move beyond stabilized permanent debt for a carefully selected sponsor and specialized property. Still, their broad advantage is disciplined, long-duration capital rather than maximum proceeds.

CMBS remains the lane for nonrecourse scale. The JPMorgan-led market is preparing the 1.77 billion dollar single-borrower refinancing on a 1.78 million-square-foot Midtown Manhattan office. That transaction is still developing, and Thursday brought no reported pricing. Investors will be watching appraisal assumptions, tenant rollover, reserves and extension rights.

The improving Manhattan operating picture helps the conversation. Third-quarter leasing exceeded 10 million square feet, available office supply fell to its lowest level since 2020, and asking rents increased. Those figures do not eliminate asset-specific office risk, but they strengthen the case that a high-quality building with durable tenancy can reach the securitized market.

For smaller multifamily borrowers, current broad indications put CMBS coupons around seven percent and higher, depending on leverage and structure. That is more expensive than the best agency or life-company execution, but CMBS can provide nonrecourse proceeds when agency eligibility, bank recourse or life-company leverage does not fit.

Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac remain the benchmark permanent lenders for stabilized apartments. There was no new major agency closing published overnight, so the new information is in the competitive set rather than a fresh headline deal. Lower-leverage Fannie and Freddie quotes remain generally in the sixes, while higher leverage widens the spread and can push execution toward seven percent.

The agencies matter to the Rahway story even though SCALE is making the construction loan. If the property stabilizes as planned, agency debt becomes a logical exit. That bridge-to-agency path is central to how debt funds underwrite apartment construction and lease-up risk.

HUD also had no new material multifamily closing in the overnight cycle. The latest meaningful execution remains Dwight Capital’s 60 million dollar FHA 223(f) loan on 194 townhomes in Davenport, Iowa. FHA 223(f) pricing is broadly in the low-to-upper sixes before mortgage insurance, while 221(d)(4) construction and permanent executions can run higher.

HUD is slower and documentation-heavy, but long amortization and fully amortizing structures can solve refinance risk in a way short bridge loans cannot. For qualifying affordable and market-rate housing, that remains a valuable alternative even when private credit wins the construction headline.

Here is the markets snapshot. The 2-year Treasury is 4.78 percent, the 5-year is 5.01, the 10-year is 5.24 and the 30-year is 5.61. Latest official SOFR is 3.90 percent. Treasuries rallied, the curve steepened, and floating-rate cost edged higher. Banks are selective, life companies favor durable cash flow, CMBS is open for the right scale, agencies remain competitive on stabilized apartments, HUD offers long duration, and debt funds are supplying visible construction capital.

One thing to watch is today’s jobs report. A softer number could extend the rally at the front of the curve, but CRE borrowers need to watch the 5-, 10- and 30-year response, not just the 2-year. If the long end resists a rally while SOFR remains near 3.90 percent, financing relief will stay uneven. If yields fall across the term structure, borrowers with live fixed-rate quotes may finally get a cleaner opening to lock.

That is Debt Desk for Friday. We will be back tomorrow with the rates, the structures and the deals that make it across the finish line.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — October 1, 2026: Campaign Pressure, Energy Permitting and Higher Long Rates
item.description: President Trump begins a 32-day midterm campaign push as Washington debates energy costs and permitting. Debt Desk examines another curve steepening, lower SOFR, a major office CMBS refinancing, and fresh bank, life-company, Freddie Mac and HUD executions.
