Good morning. It is Thursday, October first.

President Trump and Vice President JD Vance are opening the final month before the midterm elections with an unusually defensive campaign swing through Republican territory.

Trump is scheduled to travel today to Texas and Oklahoma, beginning what he says will be a 32-day push through Election Day. Vance is campaigning in Florida. Those are states Republicans normally expect to hold comfortably, but party leaders are trying to lift voter enthusiasm while competitive races threaten their control of Congress.

The president’s Oklahoma stop is also notable because it will take place on the Choctaw Nation. Presidential visits to tribal nations have been rare. The Choctaw Nation is renting the venue but says it is not sponsoring the political event. Tribal leaders have framed the visit as a chance for the administration to hear about sovereignty and the needs of people in southeastern Oklahoma.

The broader political message is about economic confidence. Republicans are confronting voter frustration over gasoline, groceries and the continuing war with Iran. Trump acknowledged Wednesday that his administration has not explained its record effectively enough. The test over the next month is whether an aggressive travel schedule can change the mood, or whether high costs remain the dominant issue.

That campaign pressure was visible in a major energy announcement at the White House. Trump said South Korea plans to invest about 54 billion dollars in a natural gas pipeline and export project in Alaska. The proposed system would run roughly 800 miles from the North Slope to a liquefied natural gas terminal in southern Alaska.

The president presented the project as moving forward, with Alaska Senator Dan Sullivan beside him. South Korean officials offered a more cautious account. They said no investment has been finalized and that any commitment depends on legal review and commercial viability.

That difference matters. A project of this size needs firm buyers, financing, permits and confidence that construction costs can be controlled over many years. The announcement gives Alaska LNG political momentum, but it is not the same as a binding investment decision. Watch for signed commercial agreements and a clearer financing structure.

Congress produced two different answers to the country’s rising demand for power. A Senate bill aimed at making large data centers bear more of the cost of grid upgrades failed to advance Wednesday. The vote was 57 to 43, three votes short of the threshold needed to move forward.

The measure would have required utility regulators to consider a federal standard for charging large power users. Democrats said that was too weak because states could decline to act. Republicans said the bill would at least force regulators to confront the cost shift. The House had approved the measure 417 to 3, but the Senate deadlock leaves the issue unresolved as data centers become a larger source of electricity demand and a larger concern for households.

At the same time, senators from both parties announced a deal on broader permitting legislation. The proposal is intended to shorten federal reviews for energy and infrastructure projects and would make data centers pay for certain grid improvements. Supporters say it could help build generation and transmission more quickly while preserving environmental protections.

The agreement will not receive a vote until after the midterms, and important disputes remain, especially over whether the administration could still obstruct wind and solar projects. Even so, a bipartisan framework is meaningful. Washington agrees that the grid needs more supply and faster approvals. It still disagrees about who pays, which technologies qualify and how binding the rules should be.

There was also a fresh election-enforcement development in Minnesota. The Justice Department announced federal charges against 10 people accused of voting illegally over the last three elections. More than 8 million ballots were cast in the state during that period.

The cases will be judged on their evidence. Their scale is also part of the story. The administration has devoted major attention to noncitizen voting, while election officials say confirmed instances are rare and have not been shown to alter national outcomes. Watch whether the prosecutions reveal an organized effort or remain a small group of individual cases.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk, where a small decline in floating-rate cost came with another increase in the benchmarks used for fixed-rate real estate loans.

The official Treasury close for September thirtieth was 4.88 percent on the 2-year, 5.09 percent on the 5-year, 5.29 percent on the 10-year and 5.64 percent on the 30-year. Compared with Tuesday, the 2-year fell one basis point, while the 5- and 10-year each rose three and the 30-year rose five.

That is another steepening day. The 10-year finished 41 basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year finished 76 basis points above it. The front end suggests slightly less pressure from the expected path of short rates. The long end is demanding more compensation for inflation, supply and duration risk.

For borrowers, the distinction is practical. A lender pricing a five-year or ten-year fixed-rate mortgage off Treasuries had to raise the base rate even if its credit spread did not move. Long-duration lenders faced the biggest adjustment. A borrower watching only the 2-year would have missed the deterioration in actual permanent-loan execution.

The latest official SOFR print is 3.88 percent for September twenty-ninth, down two basis points from the prior day. A floating-rate loan at SOFR plus 350 basis points now starts around 7.38 percent before fees, reserves or the cost of an interest-rate cap.

Two basis points is welcome, but it is not a reset of the economics. Transitional assets still need income growth, more equity or a cheaper exit to refinance cleanly. The easing in SOFR and the rise in longer Treasuries also widen the choice borrowers face: remain floating and accept near-term uncertainty, or lock a fixed rate after the long end has moved higher.

The largest fresh transaction is a proposed refinancing of a major Midtown Manhattan office. Underwriters led by JPMorgan Securities are preparing a single-borrower CMBS deal that would refinance a 1.77 billion dollar debt package on a 1.78 million-square-foot office building.

The significance is not that office risk has disappeared. It is that the securitized market can still absorb a very large, asset-specific execution when sponsorship, leasing, structure and pricing meet investor requirements. Large single-asset deals can draw buyers that would not make the same loan on a bank balance sheet. They also concentrate attention on appraisal assumptions, tenant rollover and extension rights.

Life-company capital showed up in construction lending. MetLife Investment Management provided 35.4 million dollars to build a 150,000-square-foot flex and research-and-development property in Billerica, Massachusetts, outside Boston.

Life companies are usually associated with stabilized, lower-leverage mortgages, but selected construction loans can fit when the sponsor, basis and market are strong. The deal also illustrates the difference between specialized flex space and speculative commodity office. Lenders are separating uses and locations rather than treating every workplace asset alike.

Current lender indications reinforce that selectivity. As of Wednesday morning, Northmarq showed five-year life-company multifamily coupons generally from the mid-sixes to just above seven percent, with spreads ranging roughly from the mid-one-hundreds to just over 200 basis points depending on leverage. Ten-year life-company multifamily indications were broadly in the mid-sixes.

CMBS indications were higher. Five-year multifamily and commercial executions were generally around seven percent to the mid-sevens, and ten-year indications were roughly seven percent to the high sevens. Those are broad market ranges, not commitments. Still, they show the trade: CMBS can deliver nonrecourse proceeds and tolerate stories that do not fit an agency or life-company box, but borrowers pay for that flexibility.

Banks remain active when a transaction brings deposits, tax-credit support, recourse or a strong relationship. Citizens Bank provided a 35.85 million dollar construction loan as part of a 77.61 million dollar capital stack for the rehabilitation of Paulsboro Gardens, a 150-unit affordable apartment property in southern New Jersey.

The stack combines the bank loan with a 23.73 million dollar Freddie Mac-backed tax-exempt loan originated by BWE and 18.03 million dollars of low-income housing tax-credit equity from Enterprise Community Partners. That combination is a good example of how affordable multifamily gets financed when one capital source cannot do the whole job.

The bank covers construction and renovation risk. Freddie provides long-term housing liquidity. Tax-credit equity fills the remaining gap while supporting affordability requirements. The property’s 21 buildings are scheduled for unit, accessibility, water and sewer improvements, with completion targeted for late 2027.

Agency pricing remains sensitive to leverage. Wednesday’s indications placed lower-leverage five-year Fannie Mae loans around the low-to-mid sixes, while a 75 percent leverage execution could reach roughly 6.73 to 7.03 percent. Freddie Mac’s indicated five-year fixed-rate range at 75 percent leverage was about 6.44 to 6.64 percent.

Those levels show why proceeds are often constrained by coverage before loan-to-value. A higher-leverage borrower pays a wider spread at the same time the Treasury base is rising. Owners with equity can buy a meaningfully better coupon. Owners that need maximum proceeds may have to accept pricing near seven percent or restructure the capital stack.

HUD also produced a fresh closing. Dwight Capital provided 60 million dollars under the FHA 223(f) program for the 194-unit Birchwood Grove townhome property in Davenport, Iowa. The program offers fully amortizing, long-duration financing for qualifying multifamily assets, which can be especially valuable when refinancing risk is the borrower’s main concern.

Current indications put FHA 223(f) rates around 6.15 to 6.60 percent before mortgage insurance, with terms and amortization as long as 35 years. FHA 221(d)(4) construction and permanent pricing was roughly 6.60 to 7.10 percent before mortgage insurance, with terms and amortization that can extend to 40 years.

HUD is not the fastest execution and it carries program rules, documentation and mortgage insurance. But the Davenport closing is a meaningful new development after several days without a fresh HUD transaction. It confirms that long-amortizing government-insured capital is getting deals done even as conventional benchmarks move higher.

Debt funds remain the flexible lane for bridge, conversion and lease-up risk. There was no comparably large new private-credit closing Wednesday, so the latest meaningful signal remains the recent 238 million dollar Torchlight loan on 631 apartments in Doral and the 44 million dollar Davis Companies loan for a Boston office-to-apartment conversion.

The new information is the competitive backdrop. Banks and life companies are closing selected construction loans, agencies are supporting affordable housing, and CMBS is preparing a 1.77 billion dollar office refinancing. Debt funds still have an important role, but they must win on speed, structure and proceeds when cheaper capital is willing to engage.

Here is the markets snapshot. The 2-year Treasury is 4.88 percent, the 5-year is 5.09, the 10-year is 5.29 and the 30-year is 5.64. Latest official SOFR is 3.88 percent. The curve is steeper, fixed-rate benchmarks are higher, and floating-rate cost eased slightly. Banks are lending selectively, life companies are taking carefully chosen construction and permanent risk, agencies and HUD are active in multifamily, CMBS is open for scale, and debt funds remain the solution for transitional complexity.

One thing to watch is whether today’s market preserves the split between lower short rates and higher long rates. If the 5-, 10- and 30-year yields keep climbing while SOFR drifts lower, borrowers will not receive the broad relief implied by a falling overnight rate. The next decisive move will come from economic data and the market’s judgment about inflation, federal borrowing and energy costs.

That is Debt Desk for Thursday. We will be back tomorrow with the rates, the structures and the deals that make it across the finish line.

item.title: Debt Desk — Debt Desk — September 30, 2026: AI Guardrails, Softer Confidence and Selective Credit
item.description: Major technology companies sign a voluntary AI-safety accord, consumer confidence falls, and immigration cases move through the courts. Debt Desk examines a steeper Treasury curve, steady SOFR, fresh bank and debt-fund loans, agency execution and current CMBS pricing.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It is Wednesday, September thirtieth.

President Trump and leaders from some of the country’s largest technology companies have signed a voluntary accord aimed at keeping increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems under control.

The White House agreement calls for companies to use internal safeguards, bring in independent outside auditors and establish board-level committees to review the findings. Six leading AI companies participated, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia. Trump described the arrangement as a form of industry self-policing and said the government does not want to stifle development.

The accord is a concrete step, but its voluntary nature is the central question. Several of the practices resemble commitments companies have already made, and the White House offered limited detail about enforcement if an auditor finds a serious weakness. Supporters see a faster response than formal rulemaking. Critics will ask whether firms competing to release new systems can also set and enforce their own limits.

What comes next matters more than the signing ceremony: the identity and independence of the auditors, the standards they use, what companies must disclose and whether the government creates consequences for failures. Until those pieces are visible, the accord is a framework rather than a full regulatory regime.

The latest economic data delivered a mixed message. The Labor Department said employers had 7.1 million job openings at the end of August, little changed overall but lower than the prior month. Layoffs declined, while the number of workers voluntarily quitting was roughly steady. That suggests the labor market is cooling without showing the broad job destruction that normally signals a recession.

Households sound less comfortable. The Conference Board’s consumer confidence index fell 6.7 points in September to 81.9, its lowest level since 2014. Survey responses repeatedly mentioned the cost of gasoline, goods and services. Higher energy prices tied to conflict with Iran are landing on top of already elevated living costs, while wage gains feel less reassuring to consumers.

Those two reports can coexist. Employers may still be reluctant to cut staff, even as families become more pessimistic about prices and the outlook. Friday’s employment report is the next major test. A soft but positive payroll number would support the idea of gradual cooling. A sharper miss would make the decline in confidence look more like an early warning.

Immigration policy produced two important court developments. The Supreme Court allowed the administration, for now, to continue quickly deporting people to countries other than their own while the justices consider the legality of that policy. The decision pauses a lower-court restriction and keeps the government’s process operating during the appeal.

Separately, a federal appeals court heard the Justice Department’s effort to stop a judge’s contempt investigation into whether administration officials ignored an order blocking deportation flights carrying Venezuelan migrants to El Salvador. Judges on the panel appeared skeptical of the government’s argument that the investigation should end.

The cases involve different legal questions, but together they show how much of immigration policy is being shaped through emergency orders and procedural fights. The next markers are a fuller Supreme Court ruling on third-country deportations and the appeals court’s decision on whether the contempt inquiry can continue.

There is also fresh scrutiny of federal spending on political-style advertising. The Department of Homeland Security committed 20 million dollars to a media campaign featuring President Trump. Republican and Democratic critics say the ads resemble campaign material and may violate restrictions on taxpayer-funded propaganda.

Federal contract records show the award went to a Maryland advertising agency for a national media campaign, and outside tracking indicates that at least three television ads have already aired. DHS has not accepted the critics’ characterization. The practical questions now are what account funded the campaign, how much has actually been spent and whether inspectors general, Congress or the courts intervene.

That is the national brief. Now to the Debt Desk, where the latest curve is sending different messages at the front end and the long end.

The official Treasury close for September twenty-ninth was 4.89 percent on the 2-year, 5.06 percent on the 5-year, 5.26 percent on the 10-year and 5.59 percent on the 30-year. Compared with Monday, the 2-year fell three basis points, the 5-year was unchanged, the 10-year rose two and the 30-year rose three.

That is a modest steepening move. The 10-year finished thirty-seven basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year finished seventy basis points above it. Short-rate expectations improved slightly, but investors demanded more compensation for long duration. For real estate borrowers, that means relief was limited to the front end. Five-year pricing did not improve, and ten- and thirty-year capital became a little more expensive.

The latest official SOFR print is 3.90 percent for September 28, unchanged from the prior reading. A floating-rate borrower paying SOFR plus three hundred fifty basis points still starts around 7.40 percent before fees, reserves or an interest-rate cap. Stable is better than another increase, but it does not solve the coverage problem for transitional assets carrying coupons in the sevens or higher.

Fresh lender indications published Tuesday make the execution divide visible. For moderate-leverage multifamily, indicative five-year Fannie Mae fixed-rate quotes generally ranged from the mid-sixes into the low sevens, depending on leverage and coverage. Freddie Mac indications were in a similar band. Life-company multifamily quotes were broadly in the mid-sixes to just above seven percent, while indicative CMBS coupons clustered around seven percent and higher.

These are market indications, not commitments, and property quality can move a quote substantially. Still, the hierarchy is clear. Stabilized apartments with conservative leverage can access agency or life-company money in the sixes. CMBS provides proceeds and nonrecourse execution for a wider set of properties, but the coupon can begin with a seven. Banks can compete inside those levels when a relationship, deposits or recourse support the credit.

Deals are getting done across those lanes. JPMorgan Chase provided 66.5 million dollars against the historic office building at 836 and 838 Broadway in Manhattan’s Union Square. The loan refinanced 28.9 million dollars of prior debt after the owner invested more than 20 million dollars repositioning a building it had acquired vacant.

That is bank lending with a recognizable story: substantial sponsor capital, demonstrated leasing progress and a basis that can be defended. It is not evidence that every office is financeable. It shows that banks will lend on an office asset when the borrower has already absorbed the heavy repositioning risk and the collateral has moved closer to stabilization.

Construction lending also produced a fresh closing. An affiliate of GID provided a 125 million dollar, three-year floating-rate loan for the second phase of the Edge Collective mixed-use project in St. Petersburg, Florida. The project includes a 330-unit apartment tower, and the loan is scheduled to mature roughly a year after delivery.

The structure tells the story. A floating-rate construction loan gives the developer time to build and begin lease-up, but it leaves both the operating plan and the exit exposed to SOFR. The extra year after projected completion is valuable runway, not a guarantee. Leasing pace, rent achievement and the permanent-loan market will determine whether the exit works cleanly.

Debt funds are providing the flexible capital that banks often will not. Torchlight Investors made a 238 million dollar short-term loan on the 631-unit Landmark South apartment property in Doral, Florida. The size shows that private credit remains capable of financing institutional multifamily at scale, especially when the borrower needs speed, transitional proceeds or time before permanent execution.

Another debt-fund example came from Boston, where Davis Companies provided 44 million dollars for the conversion of an older downtown office building into apartments. The lender recently formed a dedicated credit platform. Conversion loans carry construction, entitlement and lease-up risk, but they can also solve two market problems at once: obsolete office inventory and undersupplied housing.

Capital is also being raised for more of this activity. JLL launched a non-traded mortgage REIT that plans to originate and acquire commercial real estate debt. That is not a closed loan, but it is meaningful capacity. New vehicles increase competition for senior bridge, mezzanine and other credit opportunities, and they give debt funds another route to gather longer-lived capital.

Life companies remain most competitive where the story is simpler: durable cash flow, moderate leverage and a borrower willing to trade maximum proceeds for predictable execution. The latest market grid showed five- and ten-year life-company multifamily spreads varying widely with leverage. Lower-leverage ten-year quotes were indicated closer to the low-to-mid one-hundreds over Treasuries, while higher leverage required a wider premium.

The important point is that spread discipline has not disappeared just because capital is available. A life company may hold its spread while the Treasury base moves against the borrower. Tuesday’s two-basis-point rise in the 10-year therefore passes almost directly into a new fixed-rate quote unless the lender chooses to absorb it.

Multifamily had a notable agency closing. JLL Real Estate Capital provided an 86.05 million dollar Fannie Mae loan on the 400-unit Griffis Union Station apartments in downtown Denver. The five-year financing gave the owner a fresh execution in a market where higher benchmarks are reducing proceeds and making shorter fixed-rate terms attractive to borrowers who do not want to lock for a decade.

Indicative agency pricing shows the trade-off plainly. Lower leverage and stronger debt-service coverage produce the tightest spreads. Borrowers seeking more proceeds face wider spreads and, often, a coverage constraint that caps the loan before loan-to-value does. Fannie and Freddie remain dependable sources of liquidity, but dependable does not mean inexpensive.

HUD and FHA remain the long-duration alternative. Tuesday’s indicative market levels placed FHA 223(f) acquisition and refinance loans in the mid-fives before mortgage insurance, with up to thirty-five-year terms and amortization for qualifying properties. New-construction and substantial-rehabilitation execution under 221(d)(4) was indicated somewhat higher, with terms and amortization extending to forty years.

There was no fresh HUD mortgagee-letter change in the last day. The development is market pricing, not program policy. FHA can offer leverage and duration that are hard to match, particularly for affordable housing, but borrowers must weigh that benefit against mortgage insurance, documentation and a longer closing process.

CMBS is showing both sides of the market. Nomura recently originated a 270 million dollar CMBS loan on One Culver, a large office property in Culver City, California. The two-year loan includes three one-year extension options, giving the Blackstone and LBA Realty venture time to execute while placing the credit into the securitized market.

On the loss side, Bank of America Plaza in downtown St. Louis sold for 9.6 million dollars, producing a 39.1 million dollar loss to the CMBS trust that held its 42.8 million dollar loan. That outcome is a reminder that an open new-issue market can coexist with severe losses in legacy office collateral. Current lenders are underwriting today’s basis and structure; older trusts are still recognizing yesterday’s value decline.

Here is the concise markets snapshot. The 2-year Treasury is 4.89 percent, the 5-year is 5.06, the 10-year is 5.26 and the 30-year is 5.59. Latest official SOFR is 3.90 percent. Banks are lending selectively where sponsorship and leasing justify the risk. Life companies are competitive on stabilized, moderate-leverage assets. Agencies remain active in multifamily. Debt funds are funding construction, bridge and conversions. CMBS can deliver large nonrecourse executions, but legacy losses remain real.

One thing to watch is Friday’s employment report, and especially what it does to the middle and long end of the curve. Tuesday gave borrowers a small rally in the 2-year but higher 10- and 30-year yields. A softer labor print could pull fixed-rate benchmarks down. A resilient report, combined with weak consumer confidence and high energy costs, could keep the curve steep and force another round of quote revisions.

That is Debt Desk for Wednesday. We will be back tomorrow with the rates, the structures and the deals that make it across the finish line.
